proposals.title: Teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, relieves differentiation blockade in human AML through on-target DHODH inhibition at exposures separable from venetoclax–azacitidine oxidative-phosphorylation suppression.
proposals.text:
Hypothesis title: Teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, relieves differentiation blockade in human AML through on-target DHODH inhibition at exposures separable from venetoclax–azacitidine oxidative-phosphorylation suppression.

Biological context and hypothesis. The claim covers primary human AML only when viable blasts have a fraction positive for any of CD11b, CD14, or CD15 below 20% and morphologic myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and monocytes together below 10%. In that gated population, teriflunomide will induce cell-intrinsic myeloid maturation by inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) at free concentrations at or below the unbound plasma maximum of its approved multiple-sclerosis dose, with normal CD34-positive colony formation retained at or above 70% of vehicle. Samples missing the immaturity gate, and samples lacking same-sample DHODH-pathway suppression, lie outside the claim and are reported separately. Bulk differentiation, leukemia-initiating activity, ROS-low quiescent leukemia stem cells, and cytarabine-residual oxidative cells stay separate endpoints.

Supported premises. [S4] reports that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in those models, tying that result to myeloid maturation. [S4] leaves open whether an approved drug reproduces that result at suitable exposure and selectivity. [S1] reports that leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens often had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2, and that BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. [S3] connects venetoclax–azacitidine, an established regimen and mechanistic comparator, to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation changes in leukemia stem cells. Repeating that combination is not the proposed discovery. [S2] reports that cytarabine-residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells and showed oxidative-metabolism and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features, so residual disease and the ROS-low population are distinct contexts.

Speculative bridges, labeled as such. Unverified prior knowledge requiring source checking: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis and is described as a DHODH inhibitor; brequinar is the experimental DHODH inhibitor associated with the differentiation result summarized by [S4]; suppression is read as dihydroorotate accumulation and uridine-triphosphate depletion; and exogenous uridine bypasses a DHODH block. Approved dose, protein binding, free plasma Cmax, and marrow free level are unverified and must be locked from primary sources before testing. [S1]–[S4] do not establish those facts. Bridge one: multiple-sclerosis-compatible free exposure inhibits DHODH in gated blasts enough to recapitulate [S4]. Bridge two, which [S4] alone does not entail: when dihydroorotate and uridine-triphosphate changes match brequinar, maturation scales with the depth of pyrimidine-pool depletion. Bridge three: maturation is dissociable from loss of ROS-low, BCL-2-high leukemia stem cells [S1] and from the cytarabine-residual oxidative state [S2]. Bridge four: uridine rescue assigns the phenotype to DHODH rather than to off-target oxidative-phosphorylation suppression of the venetoclax–azacitidine type [S3].

Alternative explanations. These include selective death of immature blasts, proliferation arrest without lineage maturation, off-target oxidative-phosphorylation stress [S1], [S3] or use of the oxidative state in [S2], and host immunomodulation without blast-intrinsic DHODH inhibition.

Discriminating preclinical test. The numeric cutoffs below are prespecified decision thresholds, not results from [S1]–[S4]. In paired gated AML blasts and normal CD34-positive cells, and in separate ROS-low [S1] and cytarabine-residual [S2] fractions, compare teriflunomide, vehicle, brequinar, and venetoclax–azacitidine [S3], with teriflunomide capped at the pre-locked unbound plasma Cmax. Same-sample readouts are dihydroorotate and uridine triphosphate. Differentiation versus vehicle requires at least a 15-point rise in morphologic myelocytes, metamyelocytes, or monocytes and at least a twofold rise in viable cells acquiring CD11b, CD14, or CD15, at viability at least 70% of vehicle, plus a viability-matched cell-cycle comparison so G0/G1 arrest alone fails. The shift must reach at least half the brequinar morphologic and marker change at matched pathway suppression. Uridine must restore uridine triphosphate and reverse the AML differentiation and growth effects. Normal colonies must remain at or above 70% of vehicle at that AML concentration. An oxygen-consumption drop of 30% or more with viability loss is oxidative-phosphorylation suppression, scored apart from differentiation. The added positive pattern is a graded pyrimidine-pool versus maturation relationship across the series.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis fails if pathway-suppressed gated blasts miss the morphology, CD11b, CD14, CD15, and viability-matched cell-cycle criteria; if the uridine-reversible differentiation EC50 exceeds verified free plasma or marrow concentration; if uridine restores uridine triphosphate and differentiation persists; or if normal CD34-positive colonies fall below 70% of vehicle at the AML differentiation concentration. Failure of the locked free maximum to suppress dihydroorotate and uridine triphosphate falsifies the exposure bridge. Samples still unsuppressed above that ceiling lie outside the on-target claim. Uridine-resistant cytotoxicity plus ROS-low cell loss and reduced oxygen consumption reassigns the result to the comparator in [S1] and [S3] (PMIDs 23333149 and 30420752) even when a maturation marker rises. A finding limited to cytarabine-residual cells is interpreted with [S2] (PMID 28416471) and does not confirm the [S4] differentiation mechanism (PMID 27641501).

Limitations. [S4] is confined to the models studied. Genotype range inside the gate is unverified. Differentiation can transiently enlarge recognizable myeloid bulk. Cytarabine interaction is untested.

proposals.title: Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss
proposals.text:
Title: Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.

Hypothesis and context. In post-cytarabine residual AML that still shows a differentiation block, relies on de novo pyrimidine synthesis, and retains oxidative metabolism, atovaquone at a verified unbound exposure will inhibit respiratory complex III, shrink the oxidized ubiquinone pool, and thereby restrict DHODH long enough to induce genotype-confirmed myeloid maturation and lower leukemia propagation. The intended mediator is pyrimidine depletion with ATP still intact. The original indication is treatment and prophylaxis of Pneumocystis pneumonia, and atovaquone plus proguanil for malaria; those label facts, reported protein binding above 99.9%, and any mammalian complex III potency are unverified prior knowledge and must be confirmed before exposure claims are made.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant cells in the studied models were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative metabolism, and changing that state changed response [S2]. Separately, DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells are a distinct population and a selectivity benchmark [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is only the established metabolic comparator [S3]. Nothing in [S2] or [S4] shows that residual cells are DHODH-dependent or salvage-limited; that gap is a go/no-go, not an assumption.

Speculative bridges. Bridge 1: ubiquinone redox restriction will suppress DHODH before nonspecific energetic failure at unbound levels that do not exceed label-verified unbound Cmax. Bridge 2: residual cells that pass the gates below will mature, whereas normal progenitors in a matched cycling state will keep colony-forming capacity. Bridge 3: a functional respiratory chain can support DHODH, so an oxidative phenotype is a complex III entry point, while pyrimidine dependence is set by de novo-versus-salvage flux. Human DHODH use of oxidized ubiquinone, uridine bypass of de novo synthesis, and the properties of Saccharomyces cerevisiae URA1 (cytosolic, fumarate-linked, respiratory-chain-independent type 1 DHODH) are unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of leflunomide (rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide itself approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; unverified prior knowledge), is the reference DHODH inhibitor, not the repurposing claim.

Preclinical strategy. Lock gates on the same primary specimens before any atovaquone attribution. Eligibility requires a cytarabine pulse and washout, residual oxygen consumption with an etomoxir-sensitive fraction at least 1.5-fold matched pretreatment blasts, proliferation recorded as a covariate, baseline CD11b and CD14 each below 20% of genotype-confirmed cells with blast morphology, and salvage limitation defined by tracer partitioning (at least half of UTP from the de novo route) or by uridine reversing at least 70% of the reference inhibitor’s nucleotide and maturation effects. Labeled-uridine incorporation is only a cycling covariate. ROS-low leukemia stem cells [S1] and pretreatment bulk blasts are separate arms. The go/no-go requires teriflunomide, in protein-containing medium, to raise dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold and CD11b by at least 15 percentage points while ATP stays within 20% of vehicle, with uridine reversing both. Failure aborts the atovaquone test in that context. Isolated-enzyme assays must show atovaquone inhibits complex III and spares DHODH, and teriflunomide the reverse. Measure free atovaquone; the translational claim fails if the free EC50 for a twofold dihydroorotate:orotate shift exceeds label-verified unbound Cmax. A time gate must show ubiquinone reduction and pyrimidine-flux change while ATP loss is still under 20% and before maturation. Coincident ATP collapse makes the run uninterpretable and stops it. In an engineered line, induce URA1 only after the residual state is established and prove that pyrimidine restoration leaves complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact. Uridine and URA1 must first reverse teriflunomide; if either rescue fails against teriflunomide, stop. Later endpoints are morphology plus the marker panel, absolute viable counts, apoptosis, and post-washout clonogenicity. Selectivity fails if normal CD34-positive colony inhibition at the free EC50 is within threefold of AML. Only after these gates, cytarabine-primed xenografts test marrow free drug, differentiation, limiting-dilution initiating-cell frequency (prespecified threefold reduction), and normal hematopoietic recovery. A documented search must separate this residual-state, salvage-gated, ubiquinone-timed claim from any published atovaquone or leflunomide AML work; this packet does not establish novelty.

Alternatives and falsification. Apparent maturation can reflect preferential loss of immature cells, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH binding, other atovaquone targets, or ATP collapse. The relationship is falsified, even if atovaquone remains cytotoxic, if validated uridine and URA1 rescues restore pyrimidine pools and leave complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact yet differentiation and at least a threefold clonogenic loss persist, while the same rescues reverse teriflunomide.

Limitations. Protein binding may leave no unbound window; proliferating normal progenitors may be equally sensitive; differentiation need not durably clear leukemia; [S2] models may differ from clinical marrow; [S4] does not transfer across genotypes; murine pyrimidine metabolism may diverge. Exposure, construct biochemistry, and prior AML studies require external verification.

proposals.title: Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation
proposals.text:
Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation

Hypothesis: In cytarabine-residual AML with an oxidative metabolic phenotype, persistent differentiation blockade, and low functional uridine-salvage capacity, clinically achievable unbound teriflunomide exposure will inhibit DHODH, deplete pyrimidine pools, and induce durable myeloid differentiation. This should reduce leukemia-propagating capacity while relatively sparing normal hematopoietic progenitors. Low salvage capacity, rather than oxidative metabolism alone, is the proposed determinant of sensitivity.

Supported premises: DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in experimental AML systems [S4]. Cytarabine-resistant AML cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties but were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells [S2]. These findings justify investigating a differentiation-directed metabolic intervention in residual disease, but neither establishes teriflunomide efficacy. The ROS-low, BCL-2-associated stem-cell population described in [S1] must therefore be analyzed separately rather than equated with all residual AML. Venetoclax–azacitidine provides an established energy-metabolism comparator, not a new repurposing proposal [S3].

Drug premise and speculative bridges: Teriflunomide’s approval for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and its DHODH-inhibitory activity are unverified prior knowledge here; the packet does not verify either claim. Another unverified biochemical premise is that extracellular uridine salvage can replenish pyrimidines despite DHODH inhibition. Regulatory status, target pharmacology, and human unbound exposure require independent confirmation before experimentation. The central speculative bridge is that a subset of residual AML cannot salvage enough uridine under marrow conditions to compensate for DHODH inhibition. Further assumptions are that achievable drug exposure crosses this metabolic threshold, nucleotide depletion produces differentiation rather than only arrest or death, and normal progenitors retain sufficient compensatory capacity. Oxidative metabolism is not assumed to prove DHODH dependence.

Discriminating preclinical strategy: Study paired pretreatment and cytarabine-residual patient-derived AML samples, supplemented by residual-disease xenografts. Before drug treatment, measure respiration and quantify functional salvage using labeled uridine incorporation into pyrimidine nucleotides under physiologically justified uridine conditions. Include both low- and high-salvage AML, and normal donor CD34-positive progenitors. Use stromal coculture and protein-containing media, directly measure unbound drug, and restrict efficacy conclusions to independently verified human-compatible exposures. Establish temporal ordering by measuring DHODH-pathway metabolites and nucleotide pools before apoptosis, respiratory collapse, or maturation. Score differentiation using blinded morphology and mature-myeloid immunophenotypes in cells confirmed to retain the leukemia genotype; this guards against mistaking surviving normal cells or selective blast killing for malignant-cell differentiation.

Mechanistic discrimination: Compare teriflunomide with vehicle, an independently characterized DHODH inhibitor, and established venetoclax–azacitidine [S3]. DHODH suppression should phenocopy the differentiation response. Uridine supplementation should reverse differentiation when isotope tracing confirms restoration of pyrimidine pools, without reducing drug exposure. These interventions distinguish on-pathway nucleotide limitation from unrelated drug toxicity. Measure viable malignant-cell output, apoptosis, and colony formation separately. In randomized xenografts, determine free plasma and marrow exposure, then test leukemia-propagating capacity by limiting-dilution secondary transplantation after drug washout. Assess normal progenitor colony formation and normal hematopoietic engraftment in parallel; reduced AML viability alone does not demonstrate selectivity or stem-cell depletion.

Alternatives, falsification, and limitations: Apparent maturation could reflect differential survival of pre-existing mature cells, generic cytostasis, or off-target toxicity. Marrow-derived uridine could abolish a response seen in simplified culture. The central falsifying observation would be confirmed DHODH engagement and sustained pyrimidine depletion in predicted low-salvage residual AML without genuine differentiation or reduced leukemia-propagating capacity. Persistence of the response after verified pyrimidine-pool rescue would instead contradict the proposed causal mechanism. Failure to engage DHODH at human-compatible exposure would reject translational feasibility. Heterogeneous salvage capacity, microenvironmental rescue, uncertain marrow pharmacokinetics, and normal-cell toxicity remain major limitations. The packet supports a pathway rationale, not this drug’s therapeutic window, clinical benefit, or novelty.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide for differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia through dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibition
proposals.text:
The hypothesis title is Teriflunomide for differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia through dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibition. The biological context is primary or xenografted human AML whose blasts retain an immature myeloid phenotype and fail to complete granulocytic or monocytic maturation. Teriflunomide is proposed as differentiation therapy. The primary endpoint is myeloid maturation. Bulk cytotoxicity, effects on quiescent leukemia stem cells, and effects on cytarabine-residual cells are measured as mechanistic discriminators.

Unverified prior knowledge, which this packet does not establish and which must be checked against drug labels and pharmacokinetic sources, is that teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and that its principal target is dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), the enzyme oxidizing dihydroorotate in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Plasma levels, protein binding, and marrow exposure are likewise unverified prior knowledge. Venetoclax with azacitidine is used only as an established mechanistic comparator [S3].

Supported premises are confined to the packet. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in those models, connecting metabolism to differentiation rather than only to nonspecific killing [S4]. The packet summary does not identify that inhibitor as teriflunomide. Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the specimens studied by Lagadinou and colleagues often had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1]. Residual cells after cytarabine, in the models studied by Farge and colleagues, were not consistently enriched for that immature quiescent stem-cell state, but they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related oxidative metabolism [S2]. Venetoclax with azacitidine was associated with leukemia-stem-cell energy-metabolism changes, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects [S3].

The speculative bridges are three. First, teriflunomide inhibits DHODH in differentiation-arrested AML blasts at free concentrations overlapping exposures used for its approved indication. Second, on-target interruption of de novo pyrimidine synthesis is sufficient to reproduce the differentiation result in [S4]. Third, AML blasts have a wider margin for this maturation effect than normal hematopoietic progenitors. [S4] states that the pathway result does not transfer automatically to every approved drug affecting the pathway and does not establish suitable exposure or selectivity. [S1] states that a mitochondrial site of action does not establish a therapeutic window for an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor.

Alternative explanations remain open. Marker shifts can accompany nucleotide-stress death and mimic maturation. Unverified prior knowledge is that teriflunomide has been discussed for activities beyond DHODH; any off-target contribution in AML is untested. The dominant action could instead be oxidative-phosphorylation or TCA-cycle suppression of the kind associated with venetoclax-azacitidine [S3], or an effect limited to the oxidative residual state in [S2], with surface-marker changes as a secondary consequence. Sensitivity could also be restricted to genetic subsets that [S4] does not assign to this approved drug.

The discriminating preclinical test uses paired primary AML blasts and normal CD34-positive hematopoietic cells, plus one patient-derived xenograft, restricted to samples with a predeclared differentiation arrest. Target engagement is dihydroorotate accumulation together with depletion of uridine and cytidine nucleotides. The primary endpoint is a maturation program that precedes loss of viability: morphology, gain of CD11b and CD14, coherent loss of the sample's immature markers, and a myeloid-maturation transcriptional signature, recorded alongside annexin V and colony assays. Exogenous uridine is the rescue metabolite expected to restore pyrimidine pools downstream of DHODH; a control nucleoside that leaves those pools depleted is run in parallel. Oxygen consumption, TCA-cycle intermediates, and stem-cell frequency are measured in ROS-low fractions [S1] and in cytarabine-residual cultures [S2]. Venetoclax-azacitidine is included as the metabolic-suppression reference [S3]. Selectivity requires a larger maturation response in AML blasts than developmental injury in normal myeloid colonies at the same free-drug levels.

The proposed relationship is false if DHODH-engaging concentrations leave myeloid differentiation unchanged relative to vehicle, or if uridine restoration of pyrimidine pools leaves the maturation phenotype intact. It is false if the consistent effect is viability loss or oxidative-phosphorylation suppression of the [S3] pattern without a preceding maturation program. As a selective strategy, it is false if the same concentrations injure normal CD34-positive progenitors to an equal or greater degree.

Limitations follow from the packet. [S4] does not identify an approved inhibitor, a marrow-effective free concentration, or activity across every AML genotype. [S1] and [S2] separate bulk differentiation, when it occurs, from eradication of ROS-low leukemia stem cells and from reprogramming of cytarabine-residual oxidative cells. Approval status, human exposure, immunomodulatory effects of a multiple-sclerosis drug, and clinical safety require independent verification and lie outside this preclinical design.

proposals.title: Atovaquone-driven DHODH restriction induces differentiation in oxidative cytarabine-residual AML
proposals.text:
Atovaquone-driven DHODH restriction induces differentiation in oxidative cytarabine-residual AML

Hypothesis: At clinically attainable unbound exposure, atovaquone will inhibit respiratory-complex-III-supported DHODH activity sufficiently to induce differentiation and reduce leukemia propagation in cytarabine-residual AML with persistent oxidative metabolism and limited pyrimidine salvage. The predicted effect is mediated by pyrimidine depletion, rather than generalized ATP collapse. This concerns a defined residual-cell context, not all AML or an assumed leukemia-stem-cell population.

Supported premises: Cytarabine-resistant AML cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated features in the studied models, but were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells [S2]. Separately, DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems [S4]. Together, these findings motivate testing a respiratory-to-pyrimidine connection; they do not establish that oxidative residual cells are especially DHODH-dependent. The ROS-low, BCL-2-associated population described in [S1] should be assessed separately rather than used as a synonym for residual disease. Venetoclax–azacitidine provides an established metabolic comparator, not the proposed repurposing discovery [S3].

Drug rationale and speculative bridges: Unverified prior knowledge requiring independent checking is that atovaquone was originally approved for treatment of Pneumocystis pneumonia, can inhibit mammalian mitochondrial complex III under some experimental conditions, and has substantial protein binding. Also unverified within this packet are the biochemical premises that mitochondrial DHODH requires oxidized ubiquinone and that uridine salvage can bypass de novo pyrimidine synthesis. The central speculative bridge is that atovaquone-induced restriction of ubiquinone oxidation will suppress DHODH before causing nonspecific energetic failure. A second, explicitly uncertain bridge is that salvage-limited residual AML will differentiate under this restriction while normal hematopoietic progenitors retain sufficient functional capacity. Neither bridge follows automatically from an oxidative phenotype.

Discriminating preclinical strategy: Use multiple primary AML specimens exposed to a cytarabine pulse followed by washout, alongside matched untreated AML and normal marrow progenitors in comparable cycling states. Before testing response, classify residual samples by oxygen consumption and labeled-uridine incorporation, with a prespecified oxidative, salvage-low subgroup. Measure free atovaquone in protein-containing culture conditions and restrict translational conclusions to independently verified achievable unbound exposures. Early measurements should include complex III activity, ubiquinone redox state, dihydroorotate-to-orotate balance, pyrimidine-synthesis flux, nucleotide pools, ATP, and apoptosis. Separate biochemical assays of complex III and DHODH should test whether the drug acts through respiration rather than directly inhibiting DHODH.

Later endpoints should distinguish maturation from selective killing: follow leukemia-genotype-confirmed cells through morphology and a prespecified myeloid differentiation-marker panel, track absolute viable cell numbers, and assess clonogenicity after drug washout. Compare vehicle, a reference DHODH inhibitor, and venetoclax–azacitidine as the established comparator [S3]. The decisive epistasis experiments are uridine supplementation and expression of a validated respiratory-chain-independent DHODH construct. Both should restore pyrimidine pools and prevent atovaquone-induced maturation and propagation loss without restoring respiratory inhibition. Rescue performance must first be validated against the reference DHODH inhibitor. If these conditions hold, extend testing to patient-derived xenografts, measuring marrow exposure, differentiation, secondary-transplant leukemia initiation, and normal hematopoietic recovery. Reduced bulk viability alone would not establish differentiation or stem-cell elimination.

Alternatives and falsification: Apparent maturation could reflect preferential death of immature cells, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH inhibition, or unrelated atovaquone targets. Genotype-resolved cell tracking, direct enzyme assays, temporal ordering, and pyrimidine rescue distinguish these possibilities. A decisive falsifying observation would be persistent differentiation and propagation loss despite both validated rescues restoring pyrimidine pools, while the same rescues reverse the reference inhibitor’s effects. That result would reject the proposed DHODH-dependent mechanism even if atovaquone remained cytotoxic.

Limitations: Physiological uridine availability, marrow exposure, heterogeneous metabolic states, and injury to proliferating normal progenitors may eliminate any therapeutic window. Effects occurring only above achievable unbound exposure would reject translational feasibility; comparable normal-progenitor damage would reject predicted selectivity. Differentiation need not produce durable leukemia control. Approval details, human exposure, rescue-construct properties, and existing AML studies of atovaquone require verification outside this frozen packet; novelty is therefore not established.

proposals.title: Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation
proposals.text:
Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation

Hypothesis. In cytarabine-residual AML with an oxidative phenotype and persistent differentiation blockade, insufficient uridine salvage relative to pyrimidine demand permits human-compatible unbound teriflunomide exposure to inhibit DHODH, deplete pyrimidines, and induce durable maturation of initially immature malignant cells. This reduces leukemia-propagating capacity while relatively sparing normal progenitors. Salvage adequacy—not oxidative metabolism alone—is the proposed sensitivity determinant.

Supported premises. DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation in experimental AML [S4]. Cytarabine-resistant cells showed oxidative-metabolism-associated features without consistent enrichment for immature, quiescent stem cells [S2]. Consequently, residual AML and the ROS-low, BCL-2-associated stem-cell population in [S1] require separate analyses. Venetoclax–azacitidine supplies an established metabolic comparator, not a new repurposing discovery [S3]. These findings establish neither teriflunomide efficacy nor salvage-based selectivity.

Drug and novelty boundaries. Unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation: teriflunomide’s original approved indication is relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis; it inhibits DHODH; and uridine transport/uridine-cytidine kinase (UCK)-mediated salvage can bypass de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Human-compatible target inhibition, differentiation rather than arrest/death, and normal-cell compensation remain speculative bridges. Prior teriflunomide/leflunomide–AML and salvage-resistance literature requires checking before asserting novelty. The candidate distinguishing prediction is reciprocal sensitivity shifts with demand-adjusted salvage adequacy at equal DHODH engagement, not another DHODH–AML association.

Exposure and physiological constraints. Exposure feasibility is currently unquantified. Before efficacy experiments, establish a numerical licensed-dose human unbound concentration–time envelope, including steady-state peak, trough, AUC, and duration, from independently verified pharmacokinetics and binding data. Measure extracellular uridine in dilution-controlled human marrow specimens and matched plasma; predefine the observed marrow range, including its upper end. Reproduce that range and exposure envelope in protein-containing stromal coculture, measuring free drug directly. Do not increase exposure beyond the envelope to obtain efficacy. Confirm free plasma/marrow exposure in xenografts; supraclinical efficacy cannot establish feasibility.

Operational biomarker and causality. Baseline labeled-uridine incorporation alone is insufficient. Define R=C/D: C is isotope-measured absolute salvage-derived pyrimidine flux during brief reference-DHODH blockade before growth or viability changes; D is pretreatment pyrimidine demand from macromolecular incorporation plus irreversible loss, in matching per-cell-time units. Prespecify R<1 as insufficient and validate this provisional cutoff in independent samples, also analyzing R continuously. Study paired pretreatment/residual samples spanning R and respiration. Inducibly increase or decrease experimentally verified limiting uridine transport/UCK activity after residual selection. Require reciprocal sensitivity shifts at matched free drug and DHODH engagement, accounting for demand changes and drug-free controls. Repeat flux/demand measurements during treatment; expression differences alone do not demonstrate causality.

Discriminating endpoints. Include vehicle, a characterized DHODH inhibitor, DHODH suppression, and venetoclax–azacitidine, alongside normal donor CD34-positive progenitors. Establish pathway-metabolite and nucleotide changes before apoptosis or maturation. Test uridine rescue with isotope-confirmed pool restoration and unchanged drug exposure/target engagement; supraphysiological rescue is mechanistic, not evidence of marrow protection. Index-sort initially immature cells and track individual lineages longitudinally using imaging and heritable barcodes, confirming leukemia genotype in mature descendants. This excludes apparent differentiation caused solely by survival of pre-existing mature leukemic cells. Assess persistent maturation after washout through blinded morphology and myeloid immunophenotyping, separately from apoptosis, viable output, and colonies. Randomized xenografts should assess limiting-dilution secondary transplantation after verified washout using equal viable malignant-cell inputs at every dose, reporting total killing separately. Test normal colony formation and hematopoietic engraftment in parallel.

Alternatives, falsification, and limitations. Off-target toxicity, cytostasis, mature-cell selection, or microenvironmental uridine rescue could explain apparent benefit. Confirmed DHODH engagement and sustained pyrimidine depletion at permitted exposure in low-R residual AML, but neither lineage-proven differentiation nor reduced propagating frequency, would falsify the central prediction. Persistence after verified pyrimidine restoration would contradict the proposed mechanism; failure of bidirectional salvage perturbation to shift sensitivity would reject salvage adequacy as the determinant. Failure to engage DHODH within the human envelope rejects translational feasibility. Changing demand, marrow pharmacokinetics, disease heterogeneity, and normal-progenitor toxicity limit extrapolation. The packet supports a pathway rationale, not this drug’s therapeutic window, clinical benefit, or novelty.

proposals.title: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML
proposals.text:
HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML

CORE HYPOTHESIS. Teriflunomide (the active molecule corresponding to the leflunomide class; original indication: relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, with leflunomide historically approved for rheumatoid/psoriatic arthritis - approval facts are unverified prior knowledge to be confirmed against the regulatory label) reaches clinically achievable free concentrations that inhibit dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) in AML blasts. Blocking DHODH-mediated conversion of dihydroorotate to orotate (textbook biochemistry, outside-packet general knowledge) depletes de novo pyrimidine synthesis, releases the myeloid differentiation block, and drives terminal maturation with cell-cycle exit. The hypothesis is only claimed for differentiation-blocked AML contexts where the dominant residual pathology is an immature, lineage-blocked blast population; it is not a stem-cell-eradication claim and teriflunomide is not an established AML regimen.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (from the packet).
- P1 (S4, core): DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and altered disease-related endpoints in experimental AML, linking pyrimidine metabolism to the differentiative state. S4 explicitly does not establish that every approved drug acting on this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity; closing exactly that gap is the purpose of this hypothesis.
- P2 (S2, context): chemotherapy-persistent AML cells were not consistently LSC-enriched but depended on oxidative metabolism, showing that residual disease contains metabolically definable, targetable states distinct from bulk untreated biology.
- P3 (S1, framing): quiescent ROS-low leukemia stem cells were BCL-2-dependent and OXPHOS-linked, demonstrating that AML populations can carry selective metabolic liabilities (e.g., venetoclax-class sensitivity). This motivates selectivity reasoning only; it does not predict DHODH effects on LSCs.
- P4 (S3, comparator): venetoclax-azacitidine showed patient-associated TCA-cycle/OXPHOS changes in leukemia stem-enriched cells, providing an established metabolic-mechanism comparator and a biomarker template. No packet source supports teriflunomide efficacy in AML; that gap is what the hypothesis proposes to test.

EXPLICITLY SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (assumptions, not evidence).
- B1: clinically achievable free teriflunomide exceeds the DHODH inhibitory threshold in blasts. Teriflunomide is reportedly highly protein-bound with a long half-life (unverified prior knowledge); B1 is the central quantitative assumption and may fail.
- B2: blasts depend on de novo pyrimidine synthesis despite plasma uridine salvage, and normal CD34+ cells depend less, yielding a therapeutic window. Indirectly consistent with S4, but unproven for this drug and compartment.
- B3: because DHODH donates electrons into the CoQ/respiratory chain, inhibition might additionally perturb respiration in the OXPHOS-dependent residual cells of S2. Conjecture, treated only as a secondary endpoint.
- B4: differentiation induction may impair leukemia stem-cell self-renewal without direct stem-cell killing; if it does not, teriflunomide would be an add-on rather than a root-of-disease agent.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS. Reported extra-DHODH activities of the leflunomide metabolite on tyrosine kinases such as JAK3/EGFR at higher concentrations (unverified prior knowledge); nonspecific nucleotide depletion causing cytostasis, apoptosis, or marker drift rather than true maturation; mitochondrial electron-flux effects independent of pyrimidine starvation; differentiation-marker changes as artifacts of culture conditions or serum pyrimidine content.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL STRATEGY.
1) Engagement: LC-MS quantification of the dihydroorotate:orotate ratio and UTP/CTP pools in primary blast cultures from a genomically diverse panel (NPM1-mutant, FLT3-ITD, TP53-mutant, MLL-rearranged) at free-fraction-matched teriflunomide concentrations derived from label pharmacokinetics.
2) Specificity matrix: pyrimidine (uridine) rescue must abolish both metabolic and differentiative effects; DHODH overexpression or an inhibitor-resistant variant should confer resistance; a structurally unrelated DHODH inhibitor should phenocopy. Absence of rescue or genetic interaction indicates off-target action.
3) Endpoint separation: quantify CD11b/CD14/CD16 induction and NBT reduction separately from S-phase exit and apoptosis, benchmarked against a purely cytotoxic control.
4) Selectivity: normal cytokine-supported CD34+ HSPC colony-forming assays at identical free concentrations.
5) In vivo: NSG xenografts/PDX dosed to human-equivalent exposure, measuring marrow blast differentiation, DHODH-substrate accumulation, and survival; S3-inspired biomarker logic as the analytic template.
6) Only after single-agent validation, exploratory testing of teriflunomide added to an HMA or venetoclax in residual-disease protocols, using S3 as the established comparator rather than as the proposal itself.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATION. At free concentrations matching clinically achievable exposure: (a) no DHODH engagement in blasts; or (b) engagement without differentiation (only cytostasis/apoptosis); or (c) differentiation effects that are neither rescued by pyrimidines nor modified by DHODH genetic state; or (d) comparable killing of normal CD34+ colonies. Any of (a)-(d) across the panel and in vivo disproves the proposed drug-mechanism-context relationship.

LIMITATIONS. Multi-week half-life implies slow pharmacodynamics and delayed response assessment (unverified label detail); known class risks include immunosuppression, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity, all requiring label confirmation; murine xenografts poorly model human pyrimidine salvage; I cannot verify from the packet whether teriflunomide or leflunomide has been tested in AML, so if comparable data exist the novelty claim must be re-scoped; investigational DHODH inhibitors in AML development are not approved drugs and do not satisfy, nor pre-empt, the repurposing question posed here.
